name: runtime-and-scaling
title: Runtime and scaling: throughput and scaling curves for the Rust engine
question:
After the ~23x performance pass and the addition of configurable PDE
parameters, how does the viva-biofilm engine's wall-time scale with grid
size, agent population, and run duration -- and what throughput
(agent-steps/sec) does it sustain?

report.title: Runtime and scaling
report.evidence_quality: deterministic sweeps (fixed seed per config, no statistical repeats)
report.objective:
Measure wall-time and throughput across three independent scaling axes
(grid resolution, initial population, run duration) at fixed, modest
per-point step counts, and produce interactive scaling curves alongside
a throughput summary.
report.result:
Measured AFTER the reaction-diffusion coupling was made to converge
(~5-7 inner PDE solves per step, under-relaxation w=0.2), which raised
per-step cost relative to the earlier single-solve engine -- an
intentional correctness trade (see interpretation). Grid sweep (40
agents, 40 steps): 0.99 ms/step at 512 cells (16x32) to 16.97 ms/step at
12288 cells (96x128) -- sub-quadratic growth in cells, no configuration
slow (<30s threshold; worst case 0.68s). Population sweep (grid 48x64, 40
steps): 1.13 ms/step at 20 final agents to 8.26 ms/step at 320 final
agents. Duration sweep (grid 48x64, 40 agents): total wall time 0.086s at
20 steps to 1.06s at 160 steps; a linear fit of total time vs. steps gives
R^2=0.987 -- close to linear, with the small deviation because population
grows via division over a run (40 -> 640 agents over 160 steps), which
compounds per-step cost as the run lengthens. Peak throughput on this run
was ~6.0e4 agent-steps/sec (single-threaded, machine-load-dependent);
the robust, hardware-independent result is the SCALING SHAPE above, not
the absolute rate.
report.interpretation:
Scaling is well-behaved: no configuration in any of the three fixed sweeps
approached the 30s slow threshold (worst case 0.68s for the largest grid).
Grid and population scaling both show a clear, sub-quadratic cost increase
with problem size; duration scaling is near-linear (R^2=0.987, the
deviation a genuine population-growth effect, not noise). Per-step cost is
HIGHER than the pre-coupling-fix engine because the reaction-diffusion
sink<->solve now iterates to self-consistency each step instead of using a
single lagged solve -- the fix that removed a period-2 oxygen limit cycle
and made the Monod substrate limitation actually bite. This micro-benchmark
uses gentle kinetics at small fixed scale, so it sees ONLY that per-step
overhead. For realistic stiff-kinetics workloads the same fix is a large
NET speedup, not a slowdown: it bounds the otherwise near-exponential
population (e.g. the RS-vs-YS competition went from unbounded ~10^5 agents
/ killed-after-minutes to ~4k agents / ~12s over the full 21-day horizon),
because runtime there is dominated by agent count, not per-step PDE cost.

study_card.one_liner: Well-behaved sub-quadratic grid/population scaling + near-linear duration (R^2=0.987), peak ~6e4 agent-steps/sec; per-step cost reflects the converged reaction-diffusion coupling, a net win on realistic (population-bounding) workloads.
study_card.reproduces: viva-native capability (engine performance/scaling) — not a paper-figure reproduction
study_card.headline: viva capability (no paper figure). — PASS: well-scaling; per-step cost is the converged-coupling correctness trade, a large net win at realistic scale.
